Battle of Saipan. Fought in June and July nineteen forty-four in the Mariana Islands, the Battle of Saipan saw American forces capture a strategic island within striking distance of Japan itself. The battle broke Japanese will to defend further west and enabled B-29 Superfortress bombers to reach Japanese cities. It also prompted a major Japanese carrier battle that resulted in further devastation to Japanese aviation.

The island campaign lasted twenty-five days. The Japanese garrison of approximately twenty-nine thousand soldiers was led by General Yoshitsugu Saito, while the American assault force of sixty-seven thousand troops from the Army and Marines was under Vice Admiral Richmond Kelly Turner. U.S. casualties reached three thousand four hundred twenty-six killed and over ten thousand wounded. Japanese casualties totaled approximately twenty-seven thousand killed, with very few surrendering.

The island's native civilian population was estimated at thirty thousand. Over twenty thousand civilians jumped to their deaths from cliffs to avoid capture, a mass tragedy remembered as the Banzai Cliff. This campaign coincided with the Battle of the Philippine Sea from June nineteenth to twentieth, where American carrier forces annihilated remaining Japanese naval aviation. Saipan's airfields granted B-29 bombers a base within range of the Japanese home islands, especially Tokyo. The battle marked the first major engagement on an island with a large native population and demonstrated the difficulties of amphibious assault against determined defense, pointing toward the even costlier battles at Iwo Jima and Okinawa that would follow.
